# Advanced R Workshop

This student workbook uses the 50-state census-and-trends dataset. Each row is a state, and the columns include climate, parks, UFO sightings, food, hobbies, animals, and other trend scores. Our running question follows beginning R: **Do colder states have higher ice cream trend scores?**

## How to use this workbook

The worked examples have complete code to run during the workshop and keep for reference. For a one-hour session, follow the main examples with the instructor, then choose two practice challenges to try on your own. The optional reference examples are available for practice afterward. The examples demonstrate plot construction, faceting, and model output while reinforcing the distinction between association and causation.

`ice cream` is a trend score, not a measure of ice cream sales or consumption. The main question is a teaching example, not evidence that weather changes what people eat.

## Setup

Install these packages once if needed, then load them every time you start a new R session.

```{r}
# Run once in the R console if you need the packages:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "broom"))

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
```

Place the clean October 7 CSV beside this file, then load it. The `across()` step makes the four yes/no columns reliably logical, and the new label columns make plots easier to read.

The `~` symbol (called a *tilde*) has two uses here. In `across()`, it starts a short function applied to each selected column, and `.x` means the current value. In formulas later on, `outcome ~ predictor` separates the value being studied from the variable used to explain or group it. In `facet_wrap()`, the tilde introduces the variable used to make separate panels.

```{r}
census_df <- read.csv(
  "census_and_trends_data_2026-10-7.csv",
  check.names = FALSE
) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(has_nba_team, has_major_zoo, is_coastal, has_waffle_house),
      ~ tolower(as.character(.x)) == "true"
    ),
    coastal_status = if_else(is_coastal, "Coastal", "Not coastal"),
    temperature_group = if_else(
      avg_temp_f < 50,
      "Below 50°F",
      "50°F or warmer"
    ),
    zoo_status = if_else(has_major_zoo, "Major zoo", "No major zoo"),
    waffle_house_status = if_else(
      has_waffle_house,
      "Has Waffle House",
      "No Waffle House"
    )
  )

glimpse(census_df)
```

# Plotting with ggplot2

`ggplot2` builds plots in layers. The usual pattern is:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x_variable, y = y_variable)) +
  geom_name()
```

The `aes()` function chooses what each visual property represents. The `geom_` function chooses the kind of mark drawn on the graph.

## Scatterplot: `geom_point()`

Start with the plot from beginning R, then add a fitted line. Each point represents one state. Do colder states have higher ice cream trend scores?

```{r}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_temp_f, y = `ice cream`)) +
  geom_point(color = "deepskyblue4", size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Do colder states have higher ice cream trend scores?",
    subtitle = "A trend line describes association, not ice cream consumption.",
    x = "Average temperature (°F)",
    y = "Ice cream trend score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The black line summarizes a pattern across the states. It does not establish that temperatures caused the difference in trend scores.

## Line plot: `geom_line()`

Line plots work best when the x-axis has a meaningful order. States do not naturally occur in a numeric order, so first rank them from coldest to warmest.

```{r}
temperature_ranked <- census_df |>
  arrange(avg_temp_f) |>
  mutate(temperature_rank = row_number())

temperature_ranked |>
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_rank, y = avg_temp_f)) +
  geom_line(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "firebrick", size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average temperature across states",
    subtitle = "States are ordered from coldest to warmest.",
    x = "Temperature rank",
    y = "Average temperature (°F)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Bar graph: `geom_bar()`

`geom_bar()` can draw bars from values you already calculated. First count the number of states in each personality profile, then use `stat = "identity"` to tell ggplot2 that the heights are already in `number_of_states`.

```{r}
profile_counts <- census_df |>
  count(personality_profile, name = "number_of_states") |>
  arrange(desc(number_of_states))

profile_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(personality_profile, number_of_states), y = number_of_states)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "How the dataset labels state personality profiles",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of states"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Histogram: `geom_histogram()`

A histogram shows the distribution of one numeric variable. Here we ask how common different ice cream trend scores are.

```{r}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `ice cream`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "mediumpurple", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "How do ice cream trend scores vary across states?",
    x = "Ice cream trend score",
    y = "Number of states"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Box plot: `geom_boxplot()`

A box plot compares distributions across groups. This one compares ice cream trend scores for states below and above the 50°F cutoff from beginning R.

```{r}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = temperature_group, y = `ice cream`)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "gold", alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Ice cream trend scores in colder and warmer states",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Ice cream trend score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Faceting plots

Faceting creates a small plot for each subgroup. It is especially useful when one busy plot would hide important differences between groups.

## `facet_wrap()`

Use `facet_wrap()` to make one panel for each personality profile. This lets us check whether the ice-cream-and-temperature pattern looks similar in all three groups. There are only 13 states in the smallest profile, so interpret its fitted line cautiously.

```{r}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = avg_temp_f, y = `ice cream`)) +
  geom_point(color = "deepskyblue4", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ personality_profile) +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature and ice cream trends by personality profile",
    x = "Average temperature (°F)",
    y = "Ice cream trend score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## `facet_grid()`

Use `facet_grid()` when two variables define the panels. This histogram breaks ice cream scores into four combinations: coastal/not coastal and major zoo/no major zoo.

```{r}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `ice cream`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, fill = "skyblue", color = "white") +
  facet_grid(coastal_status ~ zoo_status) +
  labs(
    title = "Ice cream scores by coast and zoo status",
    x = "Ice cream trend score",
    y = "Number of states"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

When comparing facets, check whether axes are shared. Keeping the same axes makes visual comparisons fair; changing them can make small differences look dramatic.

# Statistical functions

Statistical tests can help quantify a pattern, but they do not automatically make a causal claim. The `broom` package turns many model and test results into clean data frames that work nicely with the `tidyverse`.

## T-test: `t.test()`

Do states below 50°F have a different mean ice cream trend score from warmer states? The t-test compares the means of two groups. This cutoff was chosen for the workshop and can be changed; it is not a natural divide. In the test formula, the numeric outcome goes to the left of `~` and the group goes to the right.

```{r}
ice_cream_temperature_test <- t.test(
  `ice cream` ~ temperature_group,
  data = census_df
)

ice_cream_temperature_test
```

Use `tidy()` to turn the test result into a clean one-row data frame. It shows the estimated difference, confidence interval, test statistic, and p-value.

```{r}
tidy(ice_cream_temperature_test)
```

For a compact one-line summary, `glance()` is another `broom` function that you can explore after the workshop.

## Correlation: `cor()` and `cor.test()`

The `$` symbol selects a column from a data frame. For example, `census_df$avg_temp_f` means the `avg_temp_f` column in `census_df`. When a column name has spaces, put backticks around that name, as the example below does for ice cream.

`cor()` measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship, from `-1` to `1`. A value near zero indicates little linear relationship.

```{r}
cor(census_df$avg_temp_f, census_df$`ice cream`)
```

The result is about -0.12 in this version of the dataset: the linear relationship between temperature and ice cream interest is weak. This does **not** tell us how much ice cream residents eat, or why the scores differ.

`cor.test()` examines the same pair and adds a confidence interval and a hypothesis test. Use `tidy()` to view its result as a data frame. Neither function establishes a cause.

```{r}
temperature_ice_cream_test <- cor.test(
  census_df$avg_temp_f,
  census_df$`ice cream`
)

tidy(temperature_ice_cream_test)
```

## Regression: `lm()`

Linear regression models a numeric outcome from one or more predictors. This model estimates the ice cream trend score from average temperature and coastal status. Compare its temperature coefficient with the direction of the plot.

```{r}
ice_cream_model <- lm(
  `ice cream` ~ avg_temp_f + coastal_status,
  data = census_df
)
```

Use `tidy()` to see one row per coefficient. For a compact model-level summary such as (R\^2), `glance()` is available for later exploration.

```{r}
tidy(ice_cream_model)
```

Use `augment()` to add the model's results to a row for each state. With `data = census_df`, the original columns appear beside `.fitted` (the predicted ice cream trend score) and `.resid` (the observed score minus that prediction). A positive residual means the score is higher than predicted; a negative one means it is lower. Sorting by the absolute residual brings the largest surprises, in either direction, to the top.

```{r}
ice_cream_predictions <- augment(ice_cream_model, data = census_df)

ice_cream_predictions |>
  select(state, `ice cream`, avg_temp_f, coastal_status, .fitted, .resid) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(.resid))) |>
  head(10)
```

The states at the top are the ones whose ice cream trend scores differ the most from this simple model's predictions. Ask which other variables might help explain the surprise; a large residual is not evidence of a cause.

# Optional reference examples

These examples have complete code for exploring after the one-hour workshop.

## A correlation sampler

Try several different kinds of pairings before deciding whether any pattern is interesting, plausible, or merely hilarious. This code calculates four correlations and sorts them by absolute size.

```{r}
correlation_sampler <- data.frame(
  pair = c(
    "Waffles and pancakes",
    "National parks and stargazing",
    "Pizza and board games",
    "Video games and Dungeons & Dragons"
  ),
  correlation = c(
    cor(census_df$waffles, census_df$pancakes),
    cor(census_df$national_parks_count, census_df$stargazing),
    cor(census_df$pizza, census_df$`board games`),
    cor(census_df$`video games`, census_df$`dungeons and dragons`)
  )
) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(correlation)))

correlation_sampler
```

The strongest result in a short list is not automatically important. It may be a real relationship, an accident of a small sample, a proxy for another factor, or a clue that the trend data deserves a closer look. In particular, do not conclude that playing video games prevents people from rolling a d20, or that pizza searches cause game night.

### Inspect one pairing with a plot

Here is a scatterplot for the video-games-and-Dungeons-&-Dragons pairing. A plot helps you see whether a correlation comes from a broad pattern or a few unusual states.

```{r}
census_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `video games`, y = `dungeons and dragons`)) +
  geom_point(color = "seagreen4", size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Video game and Dungeons & Dragons trend scores",
    subtitle = "A relationship is not a cultural explanation.",
    x = "Video games trend score",
    y = "Dungeons & Dragons trend score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## NBA teams and taco trend scores

This summary compares mean taco trend scores for states with and without an NBA team.

```{r}
nba_taco_summary <- census_df |>
  group_by(has_nba_team) |>
  summarise(
    average_taco_score = mean(tacos),
    number_of_states = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    nba_team_status = if_else(
      has_nba_team,
      "Has NBA team",
      "No NBA team"
    )
  )

nba_taco_summary
```

```{r}
nba_taco_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = nba_team_status, y = average_taco_score)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "tomato") +
  labs(
    title = "Average taco trend score by NBA-team status",
    subtitle = "Basketball and tacos may share an arena. Or they may not.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Average taco trend score"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The t-test quantifies the observed group difference.

```{r}
nba_taco_test <- t.test(tacos ~ has_nba_team, data = census_df)

tidy(nba_taco_test)
```

# Takeaway

Remember that a compelling plot, correlation, or p-value is a starting point for analysis. Causal claims require a research design that can rule out alternative explanations.

Because these 50 rows are states rather than a random sample of people, statistical p-values are examples of test output, not proof of a general claim about all ice cream lovers. Trend scores are not sales or consumption.
